The Equality Cases of the Weak Simplex Conjecture
A Response to Mulgund’s Open Problem 8.1

Mengwei Su    Kaiwen Yang    Hao Xu and Chih-Lin I ††thanks: M. Su and K. Yang contributed equally to this work.††thanks: M. Su is with the School of Mathematical Sciences, Tongji University, Shanghai, China (e-mail: smw@tongji.edu.cn).††thanks: K. Yang is with the School of Mathematical Sciences, Tongji University, Shanghai, China (e-mail: yangkaiwen@tongji.edu.cn).††thanks: H. Xu is with Tongji University, Shanghai, China (e-mail: hxu@tongji.edu.cn).††thanks: Chih-Lin I is with China Mobile Research Institute, Beijing, China (e-mail: icl@chinamobile.com).
Abstract

Among n+1n+1 equiprobable equal-energy signals in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} under additive white Gaussian noise with maximum-likelihood decoding, which arrangement maximizes the probability of correct decoding? The question is Shannon’s, recorded by Rice in 1950. Mulgund proved in 2026 that the regular-simplex value bounds the correct-decoding probability of every signal set at every signal-to-noise ratio, leaving open whether the simplex is the only maximizer. This paper determines the equality cases in a form stronger than uniqueness. A signal set other than a regular simplex falls strictly below the bound at every positive signal-to-noise ratio. Hence a code meeting the bound at one positive operating point is already a regular simplex, up to vertex relabeling and an orthogonal map. In probabilistic form, among the correlation matrices that signal sets induce, any matrix other than the identity gives a lower-orthant probability strictly above its independent counterpart at every finite threshold, leaving no room for a nontrivial equality. No code of ambient dimension below nn attains the bound. Under an energy budget EE with unrestricted blocklength the optimal codebook is uniquely the regular simplex of circumradius E\sqrt{E}. Every optimal codeword therefore exhausts its allowance. Equality in the Simplex Mean Width Conjecture likewise occurs only at the regular simplex. The proof strengthens the first self-convolution step of Mulgund’s argument with Royen’s correlation theorem. The single-parameter rigidity is machine-checked in Lean 4.

Index Terms: 
AWGN channel, maximum-likelihood decoding, simplex code, Gaussian maxima, Gaussian correlation inequality, stochastic domination, mean width.

I Introduction

The Weak Simplex Conjecture concerns the oldest question of signal design for the Gaussian channel. Rice reported in 1950 an observation of Shannon on the placement of n+1n+1 equiprobable equal-energy signals in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} under additive white Gaussian noise with maximum-likelihood decoding [1]. The conjectured answer is a regular simplex inscribed in the energy sphere, claimed to maximize the probability of correct decoding at every signal-to-noise ratio. Massey gave the conjecture its name in his 1988 Shannon Lecture [2].

Progress over the following seven decades was partial. Balakrishnan established asymptotic and local optimality results [3]. Landau and Slepian proved optimality in low dimensions [4]. Later work explained why their argument does not extend. The average-energy variant, the Strong Simplex Conjecture, is false. Its disproof by Steiner [5] redirected attention to the equal-energy formulation. Two announced proofs, by Goldsmith for the mean-width form [6] and by Pastore for the coding form [7], contain gaps recorded in [12, App. B]. We follow [12] in citing them as prior announcements without using their asserted conclusions.

The problem acquired a second life in convex geometry. Balitskiy, Karasev and Tsigler formulated the coding question in the language of Gaussian maxima [8]. The Simplex Mean Width Conjecture asserts that among simplices contained in the unit ball the regular simplex maximizes the mean width. Kabluchko, Litvak and Zaporozhets recast this assertion as a statement about expected maxima of correlated Gaussian variables and proved an asymptotic form of it [9]. The two questions are not on the same level. The coding question compares moment-generating functions of the Gaussian maximum at every signal-to-noise ratio, while the mean-width question compares expectations alone. Expectation is the vanishing-ratio limit of the former comparison. A resolution of the coding question therefore carries the mean-width statement with it. The converse implication is not available. Sun, Hu and Lan settled the four-variable case [11]. Litvak’s survey records the state of the art before these developments [10].

Mulgund resolved the conjecture in 2026 [12]. His stochastic-domination theorem states that whenever an (n+1)×(n+1)(n+1)\times(n+1) correlation matrix satisfies R−J/(n+1)⪰0R-J/(n+1)\succeq 0, the coordinate maximum of N⁡(0,R)N(0,R) is stochastically dominated by the maximum of n+1n+1 independent standard Gaussian variables. The theorem yields optimality of the regular simplex at every signal-to-noise ratio together with the mean-width inequality. A machine-checked Lean 4 formalization accompanies it. Its closing section poses Open Problem 8.1. The problem asks for the equality cases of the lower-orthant comparison, of the moment-generating comparison and of their coding and mean-width consequences. It asks in particular whether equality at one nontrivial threshold or one positive moment-generating parameter already forces R=IR=I. Mulgund notes that his argument does not answer this question, because the variational step produces a unique aligning tilt but neither supplies the equality cases of the product inequality nor shows that every optimal code is regular.

The classical form of this question asks for the best achievable probability of correct decoding and for one arrangement that attains it. The question left open asks for something different, the full set of arrangements that attain it. The answer decides whether the regular simplex is one good design among many or the only one.

This paper answers Open Problem 8.1 completely, in a form stronger than the question requires. Stated in the language of the channel, Theorem 3 says that a signal set other than a regular simplex is strictly worse at every positive signal-to-noise ratio. Matching the optimum at one positive operating point therefore identifies the code as a regular simplex up to an orthogonal transformation. No code in ambient dimension d<nd<n attains the regular-simplex upper bound. Under a finite energy budget with unrestricted blocklength the optimal codebook is a regular simplex of full circumradius in which every codeword spends its whole allowance. Theorem 2 is the same rigidity for the moment-generating comparison at a single positive parameter. Both rest on Theorem 1, a strictly stronger probabilistic fact. If R≠IR\neq I then the lower-orthant probability exceeds Φ​(c)n+1\Phi(c)^{n+1} at every finite threshold. No threshold remains at which a nontrivial equality could hide. Corollary 4 settles the equality case of the Simplex Mean Width Conjecture. The engine behind all of these statements is a strict version of the first normalized self-convolution step in Mulgund’s proof. For the truncated exponential factors produced by his adaptive tilting, the self-convolution turns each factor into a symmetric interval indicator. A strict symmetric rectangle inequality then yields a strictly positive deficit. Royen’s Gaussian correlation theorem [14] supplies the grouping step in its proof. The deficit survives the remaining non-strict part of the argument.

Two consequences are worth stating for signal design. The regular simplex is not one optimum among several. Every departure from it costs, at every positive signal-to-noise ratio. A numerical search over constellations therefore cannot terminate on a tie. Any tie it reports is an artifact of the numerics. The finite-energy statement sits in the model used for non-asymptotic analysis of short codes [13], where the message set is small and the binding constraint is the energy budget rather than the blocklength. In that model the optimal codebook is now pinned exactly. Moreover, the requirement that every codeword spend its full allowance is a consequence rather than a design choice.

One ingredient may be of independent interest. Lemma 9 sharpens the classical symmetric rectangle inequality of Šidák and Khatri [15, 16]. For a centered Gaussian vector with standard marginals and correlation matrix S≠IS\neq I, the probability of a symmetric rectangle strictly exceeds the product of its coordinate probabilities at every finite choice of radii. Singular SS is allowed. The classical form gives only a weak inequality. Strictness does not follow from it by approximation, since a limit of strict inequalities need not stay strict. The proof isolates a two-dimensional strict gap and carries it through the remaining coordinates with Royen’s theorem.

Section II sets up the channel model and the two translations that carry the coding question into probability and into convex geometry. Section III states the main results. Section IV fixes the inputs quoted from [12] and from Royen’s theorem. Section V proves the two strict inequalities that carry the strictness. Section VI proves the theorems and the corollary. Section VII concludes. The appendix holds the sufficient-statistic reduction used for the infinite-blocklength model.

II Channel Model and Two Translations

This section fixes the channel and records the two changes of language that the rest of the paper relies on. The coding question becomes an extremal problem for the maximum of a correlated Gaussian vector. That maximum is in turn the mean width of the simplex spanned by the signals. Both translations are known. They are restated here because the theorems are stated in the first language and proved in the second.

II-A The coding problem

A transmitter sends one of m=n+1m=n+1 equiprobable messages over the real AWGN channel by mapping message ii to a signal xi∈ℝdx_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} of unit energy, as in Fig. 1. The receiver observes

Y=λ​xI+Z,Z∼N⁡(0,Id),λ>0,Y=\lambda x_{I}+Z,\qquad Z\sim N(0,I_{d}),\ \lambda>0, (1)

where λ2\lambda^{2} is the signal-to-noise ratio. The receiver decodes by maximum likelihood. Completing the square in the Gaussian likelihood turns the decision statistic into the inner product ⟨Y,xi⟩\langle Y,x_{i}\rangle. The average probability of correct decoding becomes

Pc​(x1,…,xm,λ)=e−λ2/2m​𝔼​exp⁡{λ​max1≤i≤m​ξi},ξ∼N⁡(0,G),Gi​j=⟨xi,xj⟩.P_{c}(x_{1},\dots,x_{m};\lambda)=\frac{e^{-\lambda^{2}/2}}{m}\,\mathbb{E}\exp\Bigl\{\lambda\max_{1\leq i\leq m}\xi_{i}\Bigr\},\qquad\xi\sim N(0,G),\ G_{ij}=\langle x_{i},x_{j}\rangle. (2)

The derivation runs inside the span of the signals and does not require GG invertible. Identity (2) holds for every measurable likelihood-maximizing decoder [12, Cor. 2.6].

II-B From coding to Gaussian maxima

Identity (2) says that the code enters the error probability only through the Gram matrix GG and that the design problem is an extremal problem for the moment-generating function of the maximum of a correlated Gaussian vector. Each signal set becomes a correlation matrix. Each signal-to-noise ratio becomes a moment-generating parameter. The regular simplex becomes the Gram matrix GΔG_{\Delta} of (3) below. A normalization that adds one common Gaussian coordinate to every signal, the identity (14) below, further maps GΔG_{\Delta} to the identity matrix. The question of whether the simplex is optimal thus turns into the question of whether correlated Gaussian coordinates can beat independent ones at their own maximum.

II-C From Gaussian maxima to mean width

The same quantity is a convex-geometric functional. For a simplex KK with vertices y1,…,ymy_{1},\dots,y_{m} the support function is hK​(g)=maxi⁡⟨g,yi⟩h_{K}(g)=\max_{i}\langle g,y_{i}\rangle. Integrating in polar coordinates gives 𝔼​hK​(g)=𝔼​‖g‖​w​(K)/2\mathbb{E}h_{K}(g)=\mathbb{E}\|g\|\,w(K)/2 for g∼N⁡(0,In)g\sim N(0,I_{n}), where ww denotes mean width. The expected Gaussian maximum is therefore the mean width up to a dimensional constant. This equivalence is due to Kabluchko, Litvak and Zaporozhets [9]. In this dictionary the low signal-to-noise limit of (2) is the mean-width functional. Hence the Simplex Mean Width Conjecture is the λ→0\lambda\to 0 face of the coding problem. A statement proved for every λ>0\lambda>0 automatically covers it.

The three columns of Fig. 2 are the same optimization seen from communication, probability and geometry. The results below are stated in the first language and proved in the second. In the third they follow as corollaries.

III Main Results

Fix n≥1n\geq 1 and work with n+1n+1 coordinates. Let ϕ\phi, Φ\Phi denote the standard normal density and distribution function, 𝟏=(1,…,1)𝖳\mathbf{1}=(1,\dots,1)^{\mathsf{T}}, J=𝟏𝟏𝖳J=\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^{\mathsf{T}}, α=n/(n+1)\alpha=n/(n+1), and let

GΔ=n+1n​(I−1n+1​J)G_{\Delta}=\frac{n+1}{n}\Bigl(I-\frac{1}{n+1}J\Bigr) (3)

be the Gram matrix of the centered regular nn-simplex inscribed in the unit sphere.

Theorem 1 (Single-threshold strictness).

Let RR be an (n+1)×(n+1)(n+1)\times(n+1) correlation matrix with R−J/(n+1)⪰0R-J/(n+1)\succeq 0, possibly singular, and let X∼N⁡(0,R)X\sim N(0,R). If R≠IR\neq I, then for every finite c∈ℝc\in\mathbb{R},

ℙ{X≤c𝟏}>Φ(c)n+1.\mathbb{P}\{X\leq c\mathbf{1}\}>\Phi(c)^{n+1}.

Consequently ℙ{X≤c𝟏}=Φ(c)n+1\mathbb{P}\{X\leq c\mathbf{1}\}=\Phi(c)^{n+1} at some finite cc if and only if R=IR=I.

Theorem 2 (Single-parameter rigidity of the MGF comparison).

Let GG be any (n+1)×(n+1)(n+1)\times(n+1) correlation matrix, ξ∼N⁡(0,G)\xi\sim N(0,G) and ξΔ∼N⁡(0,GΔ)\xi^{\Delta}\sim N(0,G_{\Delta}). For every λ>0\lambda>0,

𝔼​eλ​maxi​ξi≤𝔼​eλ​maxi​ξiΔ,\mathbb{E}e^{\lambda\max_{i}\xi_{i}}\leq\mathbb{E}e^{\lambda\max_{i}\xi^{\Delta}_{i}},

and equality holds at some, equivalently every, λ>0\lambda>0 if and only if G=GΔG=G_{\Delta}. If G≠GΔG\neq G_{\Delta} the inequality is strict at every λ>0\lambda>0.

Theorem 3 (Coding consequences).

Consider n+1n+1 equiprobable messages and unit signals x1,…,xn+1∈ℝdx_{1},\dots,x_{n+1}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} observed as Y=λ​xI+ZY=\lambda x_{I}+Z, Z∼N⁡(0,Id)Z\sim N(0,I_{d}), λ>0\lambda>0.

  1. (a)

    The probability of correct Bayes-optimal decoding attains the regular-simplex value at some λ>0\lambda>0 if and only if the code is a centered regular nn-simplex inscribed in the unit sphere, up to vertex relabeling and orthogonal maps of the ambient space. If d<nd<n the regular-simplex bound is strict for every code and every λ>0\lambda>0.

  2. (b)

    In the deterministic no-feedback infinite-sequence AWGN model with noise variance N0/2>0N_{0}/2>0, n+1n+1 equiprobable messages, unrestricted channel uses and per-codeword energy at most E>0E>0, the optimal probability of correct decoding equals Sreg​(E)S_{\mathrm{reg}}(\sqrt{E}), the regular-simplex value at circumradius E\sqrt{E}, and a codebook attains it if and only if ∑ici=0\sum_{i}c_{i}=0, ‖ci‖2=E\|c_{i}\|^{2}=E and ⟨ci,cj⟩=−E/n\langle c_{i},c_{j}\rangle=-E/n for i≠ji\neq j. In particular every optimal codeword uses full energy.

Corollary 4 (Equality case of the Simplex Mean Width Conjecture).

Let K⊂B2nK\subset B_{2}^{n} be an nn-dimensional simplex and Δn\Delta_{n} a regular simplex inscribed in Sn−1S^{n-1} with centroid at the origin. Then w⁡(K)≤w⁡(Δn)w(K)\leq w(\Delta_{n}), and w⁡(K)=w⁡(Δn)w(K)=w(\Delta_{n}) if and only if K=U​ΔnK=U\Delta_{n} for some U∈O⁡(n)U\in O(n). The inequality itself is [12, Cor. 2.5]. Only the equality case is proved here.

III-A A worked example

One family makes the statements above concrete and is computable in closed form. Call a signal set equicorrelated when all pairwise inner products share one value ρ\rho. The family is feasible for −1/n≤ρ<1-1/n\leq\rho<1 and contains the regular simplex exactly at ρ=−1/n\rho=-1/n. Sending x1x_{1} and comparing scores, the nn differences are ⟨Y,x1−xj⟩=λ⁡(1−ρ)+⟨Z,x1−xj⟩\langle Y,x_{1}-x_{j}\rangle=\lambda(1-\rho)+\langle Z,x_{1}-x_{j}\rangle. The Gaussian part has covariance (1−ρ)​(I+J)(1-\rho)(I+J). It can be written as 1−ρ​(V+Uj)\sqrt{1-\rho}\,(V+U_{j}) with V,U1,…,UnV,U_{1},\dots,U_{n} independent standard normal. Dividing by 1−ρ\sqrt{1-\rho} leaves

Pc=𝔼​Φ​(W+λ​1−ρ)n,W∼N⁡(0,1).P_{c}=\mathbb{E}\,\Phi\bigl(W+\lambda\sqrt{1-\rho}\bigr)^{n},\qquad W\sim N(0,1). (4)

Since Φ\Phi is increasing, (4) is strictly increasing in λ​1−ρ\lambda\sqrt{1-\rho}. The factor 1−ρ\sqrt{1-\rho} is largest at the smallest feasible ρ\rho. Inside this family the regular simplex therefore wins strictly at every signal-to-noise ratio. This proves Theorem 3(a) for equicorrelated codes in three lines. Figs. 3 and 4 plot (4) and its probabilistic counterpart. The general case is not reachable this way, since a general Gram matrix admits no such one-dimensional reduction. Supplying that is the task of the rest of the paper. Neither figure is part of a proof. Both are computed by quadrature rather than simulation.

Remark 1 (Machine-checked companion).

A Lean 4 companion, built on the formalization accompanying [12] whose axiom audit we reproduced independently, verifies the single-parameter moment-generating rigidity along an independent route with two steps. Stochastic domination combined with equality of one strictly increasing moment forces equality of laws. A correlated Gaussian vector whose maximum carries the independent distribution at all thresholds is independent. Every public declaration depends only on the three standard Lean axioms. The companion is at https://github.com/Tongji708A/simplex-uniqueness-lean, commit 6a4f340, is pinned to Lean 4.31.0 and mathlib v4.31.0 with the dependency fixed at an exact revision, builds with a single lake build. Its axiom audit is a source file whose expected output is recorded in the repository. The single-threshold statement of Theorem 1 rests additionally on Royen’s theorem. No formalization of that theorem exists to date. Its grouping step reduces to the slab-against-convex Khatri–Šidák case, a plausible target for future formalization.

V Two Strict Inequalities

Theorem 1 rests on two inequalities proved here. The first sharpens a classical Gaussian rectangle bound. The second applies it to the truncated exponential factors that Mulgund’s adaptive tilting produces.

V-A A strict symmetric rectangle inequality

The first of the two inequalities behind Theorem 1 is a strict form of the Šidák–Khatri rectangle inequality, stated here in the generality in which it is used and in which it may serve elsewhere.

Lemma 9.

Let V=(V1,…,Vn+1)V=(V_{1},\dots,V_{n+1}) be a centered Gaussian vector with N⁡(0,1)N(0,1) marginals and correlation matrix S≠IS\neq I, possibly singular. Then for all finite r1,…,rn+1∈(0,∞)r_{1},\dots,r_{n+1}\in(0,\infty),

ℙ{|Vi|≤ri, 1≤i≤n+1}>∏i=1n+1ℙ{|Z|≤ri}.\mathbb{P}\{|V_{i}|\leq r_{i},\ 1\leq i\leq n+1\}>\prod_{i=1}^{n+1}\mathbb{P}\{|Z|\leq r_{i}\}. (8)
Proof.

Since S≠IS\neq I with unit diagonal there are i≠ji\neq j with ρ=Si​j≠0\rho=S_{ij}\neq 0. We first prove two-dimensional strictness. Let (Y1,Y2)(Y_{1},Y_{2}) be standard bivariate Gaussian with correlation ρ\rho and fix r,s>0r,s>0. ℙ{|Y1|≤r,|Y2|≤s}=𝔼[𝟏{W≤r}q(W)],𝔼q(W)=ℙ{|Y2|≤s}.\mathbb{P}\{|Y_{1}|\leq r,\,|Y_{2}|\leq s\}=\mathbb{E}\bigl[\mathbf{1}_{\{W\leq r\}}q(W)\bigr],\qquad\mathbb{E}q(W)=\mathbb{P}\{|Y_{2}|\leq s\}.

For w>0w>0,

q′​(w)=ρ0σ​[ϕ⁡(s+ρ0​wσ)−ϕ⁡(s−ρ0​wσ)]<0,q^{\prime}(w)=\frac{\rho_{0}}{\sigma}\Bigl[\phi\Bigl(\frac{s+\rho_{0}w}{\sigma}\Bigr)-\phi\Bigl(\frac{s-\rho_{0}w}{\sigma}\Bigr)\Bigr]<0,

whose integrand is everywhere nonnegative and strictly positive on the positive-probability event {W<r<W′}\{W<r<W^{\prime}\}. Hence

ℙ{|Y1|≤r,|Y2|≤s}>ℙ{|Y1|≤r}ℙ{|Y2|≤s}.\mathbb{P}\{|Y_{1}|\leq r,\,|Y_{2}|\leq s\}>\mathbb{P}\{|Y_{1}|\leq r\}\mathbb{P}\{|Y_{2}|\leq s\}. (9)

If |ρ|=1|\rho|=1 then Y2=±Y1Y_{2}=\pm Y_{1} almost surely and, with p(t)=ℙ{|Z|≤t}p(t)=\mathbb{P}\{|Z|\leq t\}, the left side equals p⁡(min⁡(r,s))p(\min(r,s)). This minimum exceeds p⁡(r)​p​(s)p(r)p(s) because both factors lie in (0,1)(0,1). Hence (9) holds for all ρ≠0\rho\neq 0.

In n+1n+1 dimensions set A={|Vi|≤ri,|Vj|≤rj}A=\{|V_{i}|\leq r_{i},\,|V_{j}|\leq r_{j}\} and Bk={|Vk|≤rk}B_{k}=\{|V_{k}|\leq r_{k}\} for k≠i,jk\neq i,j. These sets and their finite intersections are symmetric and convex. Recursive application of Royen’s theorem gives

ℙ⁡(A∩⋂k≠i,jBk)≥ℙ⁡(A)​∏k≠i,jℙ⁡(Bk),\mathbb{P}\Bigl(A\cap\bigcap_{k\neq i,j}B_{k}\Bigr)\geq\mathbb{P}(A)\prod_{k\neq i,j}\mathbb{P}(B_{k}),

and all ℙ⁡(Bk)\mathbb{P}(B_{k}) are strictly positive. Combining this with (9) proves (8) for nonsingular laws. If SS is singular, write V=T​YV=TY with Y∼N⁡(0,Irank​S)Y\sim N(0,I_{\mathrm{rank}\,S}) and T​T𝖳=STT^{\mathsf{T}}=S. Replace each set by its preimage under TT. Preimages of symmetric convex sets under a linear map are symmetric convex. Royen’s theorem then applies directly in the nondegenerate space of YY. Bivariate marginals with |ρ|<1|\rho|<1 and |ρ|=1|\rho|=1 are both covered above. The singular case therefore introduces no gap. A positive-definite approximation is deliberately avoided, since limits of strict inequalities need not stay strict. ∎

V-B A strict product inequality for truncated exponentials

Lemma 10.

Let S≠IS\neq I be any (n+1)×(n+1)(n+1)\times(n+1) correlation matrix and Y∼N⁡(0,S)Y\sim N(0,S). For each ii let ai>0a_{i}>0, bi>0b_{i}>0, set fi(z)=eai​z𝟏(−∞,bi](z)f_{i}(z)=e^{a_{i}z}\mathbf{1}_{(-\infty,b_{i}]}(z), and assume ∫z​fi​(z)​d​γ1​(z)=0\int zf_{i}(z)\,d\gamma_{1}(z)=0. Then

𝔼​∏i=1n+1fi​(Yi)>∏i=1n+1∫fi​d​γ1.\mathbb{E}\prod_{i=1}^{n+1}f_{i}(Y_{i})>\prod_{i=1}^{n+1}\int f_{i}\,d\gamma_{1}. (10)

Singular SS is allowed.

Proof.

Each fif_{i} is bounded by eai​bie^{a_{i}b_{i}}, Borel, log-concave, strictly positive on (−∞,bi](-\infty,b_{i}]. The mass μi=∫fi​d​γ1\mu_{i}=\int f_{i}\,d\gamma_{1} lies in (0,∞)(0,\infty). Normalize hi=fi/μih_{i}=f_{i}/\mu_{i}. With the normalized self-convolution

(D​h)​(u)=∫ℝh⁡(u+v2)​h​(u−v2)​d​γ1​(v),(Dh)(u)=\int_{\mathbb{R}}h\Bigl(\frac{u+v}{\sqrt{2}}\Bigr)h\Bigl(\frac{u-v}{\sqrt{2}}\Bigr)\,d\gamma_{1}(v),

set Q0=𝔼S​∏ihi​(Yi)Q_{0}=\mathbb{E}_{S}\prod_{i}h_{i}(Y_{i}) and Q1=𝔼S​∏i(D​hi)​(Yi)Q_{1}=\mathbb{E}_{S}\prod_{i}(Dh_{i})(Y_{i}). Take independent Y,Y′∼N⁡(0,S)Y,Y^{\prime}\sim N(0,S) and put U=(Y+Y′)/2U=(Y+Y^{\prime})/\sqrt{2} and V=(Y−Y′)/2V=(Y-Y^{\prime})/\sqrt{2}. Then UU and VV are independent, each N⁡(0,S)N(0,S). They satisfy

Q02=𝔼U​𝔼V​∏igi,Ui​(Vi),gi,u​(v)=hi​(u+v2)​hi​(u−v2).Q_{0}^{2}=\mathbb{E}_{U}\mathbb{E}_{V}\prod_{i}g_{i,U_{i}}(V_{i}),\qquad g_{i,u}(v)=h_{i}\Bigl(\frac{u+v}{\sqrt{2}}\Bigr)h_{i}\Bigl(\frac{u-v}{\sqrt{2}}\Bigr). (11)

The exponential part cancels in vv, leaving for 2​bi−u>0\sqrt{2}\,b_{i}-u>0

gi,u(v)=μi−2e2​ai​u 1{|v|≤2bi−u},g_{i,u}(v)=\mu_{i}^{-2}e^{\sqrt{2}\,a_{i}u}\,\mathbf{1}_{\{|v|\leq\sqrt{2}\,b_{i}-u\}}, (12)

a symmetric interval indicator up to a positive factor. The set E={ui<2bi, 1≤i≤n+1}E=\{u_{i}<\sqrt{2}\,b_{i},\ 1\leq i\leq n+1\} has positive UU-probability, because all bi>0b_{i}>0 and UU concentrates near the origin with positive probability. On EE, Lemma 9 applied to V∼N⁡(0,S)V\sim N(0,S) with radii 2​bi−ui>0\sqrt{2}\,b_{i}-u_{i}>0 gives

𝔼V​∏igi,ui​(Vi)>∏i∫gi,ui​d​γ1=∏i(D​hi)​(ui)(u∈E).\mathbb{E}_{V}\prod_{i}g_{i,u_{i}}(V_{i})>\prod_{i}\int g_{i,u_{i}}\,d\gamma_{1}=\prod_{i}(Dh_{i})(u_{i})\qquad(u\in E).

Off EE at least one radius is nonpositive. A negative radius kills the corresponding factor identically. A zero radius gives zero on both sides because ViV_{i} has no atoms. Writing Δ⁡(u)=𝔼V​∏igi,ui​(Vi)−∏i(D​hi)​(ui)\Delta(u)=\mathbb{E}_{V}\prod_{i}g_{i,u_{i}}(V_{i})-\prod_{i}(Dh_{i})(u_{i}), the function Δ\Delta is measurable, bounded by 2​∏i‖hi‖∞22\prod_{i}\|h_{i}\|_{\infty}^{2}, vanishes on EcE^{c} and is strictly positive on EE. Therefore

Q02−Q1=𝔼​Δ​(U)>0.Q_{0}^{2}-Q_{1}=\mathbb{E}\,\Delta(U)>0. (13)

Each D​hiDh_{i} is bounded, log-concave by Prékopa’s theorem [17], has unit Gaussian integral and zero Gaussian first moment. Proposition 6 therefore applies to the D​hiDh_{i} and gives Q1≥1Q_{1}\geq 1. With (13), Q02>1Q_{0}^{2}>1, hence Q0>1Q_{0}>1. Unnormalizing yields (10). The argument is not circular, because Proposition 6 is Mulgund’s independently proved non-strict theorem and strictness is injected only in the first self-convolution step. ∎

VI Proofs of the Main Results

The three theorems and the corollary are proved in turn. Each proof assembles the two inequalities of the previous section with the inputs quoted in Section IV.

VI-A Theorem 1

Fix a finite cc. Proposition 7 supplies finite sis_{i} with ai=r⁡(si)>0a_{i}=r(s_{i})>0 and bi=H⁡(si)>0b_{i}=H(s_{i})>0, the positivity of bib_{i} coming from the range (0,∞)(0,\infty) of HH. Define fi(z)=eai​z𝟏(−∞,bi](z)f_{i}(z)=e^{a_{i}z}\mathbf{1}_{(-\infty,b_{i}]}(z). Equation (6) then gives ∫fi​d​γ1=eai2/2​Φ​(si)\int f_{i}\,d\gamma_{1}=e^{a_{i}^{2}/2}\Phi(s_{i}) and ∫z​fi​d​γ1=0\int zf_{i}\,d\gamma_{1}=0. If R≠IR\neq I, Lemma 10 gives

𝔼[ea𝖳​X𝟏{X≤b}]>e‖a‖2/2∏iΦ(si).\mathbb{E}\bigl[e^{a^{\mathsf{T}}X}\mathbf{1}_{\{X\leq b\}}\bigr]>e^{\|a\|^{2}/2}\prod_{i}\Phi(s_{i}).

Applying Proposition 8 with F=𝟏{x≤b}F=\mathbf{1}_{\{x\leq b\}} and using b−R​a=s+a−R​a=c​𝟏b-Ra=s+a-Ra=c\mathbf{1} from (7),

ℙ{X≤c𝟏}=e−a𝖳Ra/2𝔼[ea𝖳​X𝟏{X≤b}]>exp{∑ilogΦ(si)+12a𝖳(I−R)a}≥Φ(c)n+1,\mathbb{P}\{X\leq c\mathbf{1}\}=e^{-a^{\mathsf{T}}Ra/2}\,\mathbb{E}\bigl[e^{a^{\mathsf{T}}X}\mathbf{1}_{\{X\leq b\}}\bigr]>\exp\Bigl\{\sum_{i}\log\Phi(s_{i})+\tfrac{1}{2}a^{\mathsf{T}}(I-R)a\Bigr\}\geq\Phi(c)^{n+1},

the last step by (7). The change-of-measure factor is strictly positive. Strictness survives. If R=IR=I the coordinates are independent and equality holds at every cc. ■\blacksquare

Remark 2.

The variational inequality in (7) alone cannot prove the theorem. Its equality case is R​𝟏=𝟏R\mathbf{1}=\mathbf{1}. For n≥3n\geq 3 the condition R​𝟏=𝟏R\mathbf{1}=\mathbf{1} does not force R=IR=I. The exclusion of all remaining matrices is carried entirely by Lemma 10.

VI-B Theorem 2

Let MX=maxi⁡XiM_{X}=\max_{i}X_{i} and MZ=maxi⁡ZiM_{Z}=\max_{i}Z_{i} with Z∼N⁡(0,I)Z\sim N(0,I). Both exponential moments are finite since eμ​M≤∑ieμ​Xie^{\mu M}\leq\sum_{i}e^{\mu X_{i}}. If R≠IR\neq I, Theorem 1 gives FX​(u)>FZ​(u)F_{X}(u)>F_{Z}(u) for every uu, where FF denotes the distribution function of the corresponding maximum. The tail representation gives

𝔼​eμ​MZ−𝔼​eμ​MX=limε↓0∫ε∞(FX​(log⁡tμ)−FZ​(log⁡tμ))​𝑑t>0\mathbb{E}e^{\mu M_{Z}}-\mathbb{E}e^{\mu M_{X}}=\lim_{\varepsilon\downarrow 0}\int_{\varepsilon}^{\infty}\Bigl(F_{X}\Bigl(\frac{\log t}{\mu}\Bigr)-F_{Z}\Bigl(\frac{\log t}{\mu}\Bigr)\Bigr)dt>0

for every μ>0\mu>0, the strict sign visible on any compact [a,b]⊂(0,∞)[a,b]\subset(0,\infty) where the integrand is everywhere positive.

For a general correlation matrix GG put R=α​G+J/(n+1)R=\alpha G+J/(n+1), take B∼N⁡(0,1/n)B\sim N(0,1/n) independent of ξ∼N⁡(0,G)\xi\sim N(0,G) and set Xi=α​(ξi+B)X_{i}=\sqrt{\alpha}(\xi_{i}+B), so that X∼N⁡(0,R)X\sim N(0,R) and, for μ=λ/α\mu=\lambda/\sqrt{\alpha},

𝔼​eμ​MX=eλ2/(2​n)​𝔼​eλ​maxi​ξi.\mathbb{E}e^{\mu M_{X}}=e^{\lambda^{2}/(2n)}\,\mathbb{E}e^{\lambda\max_{i}\xi_{i}}. (14)

The same construction for GΔG_{\Delta} produces exactly R=IR=I. Since α>0\alpha>0, R=IR=I if and only if G=GΔG=G_{\Delta}. Combining (14) with the strict comparison above proves the theorem. ■\blacksquare

VI-C Theorem 3

The two parts of the theorem are proved separately. The equal-energy case follows from Theorem 2 once the Gram matrix is identified. The finite-energy case reduces to it after an exact sufficient statistic removes the infinite blocklength.

Equal energy

For unit signals the Bayes-optimal probability of correct decoding is given by (2), whose prefactor does not depend on the code. By Theorem 2 equality at any λ>0\lambda>0 holds if and only if G=GΔG=G_{\Delta}. The condition G=GΔG=G_{\Delta} forces ⟨xi,xj⟩=−1/n\langle x_{i},x_{j}\rangle=-1/n for i≠ji\neq j and ∑ixi=0\sum_{i}x_{i}=0. Fixing reference vertices uiu_{i} with the same Gram matrix, the correspondence ∑iai​ui↦∑iai​xi\sum_{i}a_{i}u_{i}\mapsto\sum_{i}a_{i}x_{i} is well defined and inner-product preserving. After completing orthonormal bases it extends to an orthogonal map of the ambient space. The code is therefore the centered regular simplex up to relabeling and ambient isometry. If d<nd<n then rank​G≤d<n=rank​GΔ\mathrm{rank}\,G\leq d<n=\mathrm{rank}\,G_{\Delta}. Equality is therefore impossible and the bound is strict at every λ\lambda. Finally, on the regular simplex the maximum-likelihood scores of two distinct messages tie only on a finite union of hyperplanes, a null set under every output law. Any Bayes-optimal decoder agrees almost everywhere with maximum-likelihood decoding.

Finite total energy

The infinite-sequence model is reduced to finitely many dimensions by an exact sufficient statistic.

Lemma 11.

In the model of Theorem 3(b) with codewords ci∈ℓ2c_{i}\in\ell_{2}, let D=span⁡{ci−c1}D=\mathrm{span}\{c_{i}-c_{1}\}, r=dimDr=\dim D, and let u1,…,uru_{1},\dots,u_{r} be an orthonormal basis of DD. The limits Tj​(Y)=limN∑k≤Nuj,k​YkT_{j}(Y)=\lim_{N}\sum_{k\leq N}u_{j,k}Y_{k} exist almost surely and in L2L^{2} under every message law, are jointly Gaussian with T(Y)∣{I=i}∼N((⟨ci,uj⟩)j,σ2Ir)T(Y)\mid\{I=i\}\sim N((\langle c_{i},u_{j}\rangle)_{j},\sigma^{2}I_{r}), and TT is sufficient; the sequence experiment and the rr-dimensional Gaussian shift experiment have the same optimal probability of correct decoding.

Proof.

See Appendix VII. ∎

For the assembly, let Sreg​(r)S_{\mathrm{reg}}(r) denote the optimal correct probability of the centered regular simplex of circumradius rr. It evaluates to

Sreg​(r)=pn+1​(r​2​(n+1)n​N0),pn+1​(a)=𝔼​Φ​(W+a)n,W∼N⁡(0,1),S_{\mathrm{reg}}(r)=p_{n+1}\Bigl(r\sqrt{\tfrac{2(n+1)}{nN_{0}}}\Bigr),\qquad p_{n+1}(a)=\mathbb{E}\,\Phi(W+a)^{n},\ W\sim N(0,1), (15)

and SregS_{\mathrm{reg}} is strictly increasing, by differentiation under the integral.

Let C={ci}C=\{c_{i}\} be an arbitrary feasible codebook. Augment each codeword by one extra coordinate, c~i=(ci,qi)\tilde{c}_{i}=(c_{i},q_{i}) with qi=E−‖ci‖2q_{i}=\sqrt{E-\|c_{i}\|^{2}}, so that ‖c~i‖2=E\|\tilde{c}_{i}\|^{2}=E. The augmented codebook C~\tilde{C} is feasible because channel uses are unrestricted and a fixed coordinate rearrangement leaves the i.i.d. noise law invariant. It satisfies S⁡(C)≤S⁡(C~)S(C)\leq S(\tilde{C}) because a decoder may ignore the extra coordinate. Let D~=span⁡{c~i−c~1}\tilde{D}=\mathrm{span}\{\tilde{c}_{i}-\tilde{c}_{1}\}, write c~i=w+vi\tilde{c}_{i}=w+v_{i} with ww the common projection onto D~⟂\tilde{D}^{\perp} and vi∈D~v_{i}\in\tilde{D}. All viv_{i} then share one radius r∗r_{\ast} with r∗2=E−‖w‖2r_{\ast}^{2}=E-\|w\|^{2}. If r∗=0r_{\ast}=0 the effective means coincide and the correct probability is 1/(n+1)1/(n+1), below the regular-simplex value. For r∗>0r_{\ast}>0, normalizing xi=vi/r∗x_{i}=v_{i}/r_{\ast} and applying (2) inside D~\tilde{D} with λ=r∗/σ\lambda=r_{\ast}/\sigma, Theorem 2 gives S⁡(C~)≤Sreg​(r∗)≤Sreg​(E)S(\tilde{C})\leq S_{\mathrm{reg}}(r_{\ast})\leq S_{\mathrm{reg}}(\sqrt{E}), the second inequality strict for r∗<Er_{\ast}<\sqrt{E} by (15). Every feasible codebook therefore satisfies S​(C)≤Sreg​(E)S(C)\leq S_{\mathrm{reg}}(\sqrt{E}). The regular simplex of circumradius E\sqrt{E} is feasible and attains this value. Hence Pc∗​(E,n+1)=Sreg​(E)P^{*}_{c}(E,n+1)=S_{\mathrm{reg}}(\sqrt{E}), attained by the regular simplex.

Now let CC attain the optimum. Every inequality above is then an equality. The case r∗=0r_{\ast}=0 is excluded because 1/(n+1)<Sreg​(E)1/(n+1)<S_{\mathrm{reg}}(\sqrt{E}) for E>0E>0. Strict monotonicity of SregS_{\mathrm{reg}} forces r∗=Er_{\ast}=\sqrt{E}, hence w=0w=0. Equality in the MGF comparison forces Gram⁡(x1,…,xn+1)=GΔ\mathrm{Gram}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n+1})=G_{\Delta} and ∑ixi=0\sum_{i}x_{i}=0 by Theorem 2. Then ∑ic~i=(n+1)​w+r∗​∑ixi=0\sum_{i}\tilde{c}_{i}=(n+1)w+r_{\ast}\sum_{i}x_{i}=0. The last coordinate reads ∑iqi=0\sum_{i}q_{i}=0 with every qi≥0q_{i}\geq 0. Hence all qi=0q_{i}=0. Every codeword uses full energy and the codebook satisfies the stated Gram conditions. Conversely any such codebook is a centered regular simplex of circumradius E\sqrt{E} and attains Sreg​(E)S_{\mathrm{reg}}(\sqrt{E}). A common translation is excluded by averaging the energy constraint. ■\blacksquare

VI-D Corollary 4

Write K=conv⁡{y1,…,yn+1}⊂B2nK=\mathrm{conv}\{y_{1},\dots,y_{n+1}\}\subset B_{2}^{n} and σi=1−‖yi‖2\sigma_{i}=\sqrt{1-\|y_{i}\|^{2}}. Lifting xi=(yi,σi​ei)x_{i}=(y_{i},\sigma_{i}e_{i}) to unit vectors and conditioning on g∼N⁡(0,In)g\sim N(0,I_{n}), the two-case Jensen argument, 𝔼​max⁡(Y,C)−max⁡(aj,C)\mathbb{E}\max(Y,C)-\max(a_{j},C) equals 𝔼​(Y−C)+>0\mathbb{E}(Y-C)^{+}>0 when aj≤Ca_{j}\leq C and 𝔼​(C−Y)+>0\mathbb{E}(C-Y)^{+}>0 when aj>Ca_{j}>C for the nondegenerate normal Y=aj+σj​WjY=a_{j}+\sigma_{j}W_{j}, shows that any vertex strictly inside the ball produces a strict gap in expected Gaussian maxima. Mean-width equality therefore forces all vertices onto the sphere. On the sphere, put G=(⟨yi,yj⟩)G=(\langle y_{i},y_{j}\rangle) and Xi=α​(ξi+B)X_{i}=\sqrt{\alpha}(\xi_{i}+B) with B∼N⁡(0,1/n)B\sim N(0,1/n) independent of ξ\xi, as in (14). If G≠GΔG\neq G_{\Delta} then R≠IR\neq I and Theorem 1 gives a strict gap between the distribution functions of the maxima at every point, hence 𝔼​MX<𝔼​MZ\mathbb{E}M_{X}<\mathbb{E}M_{Z} by integrating the gap, contradicting mean-width equality through the polar decomposition 𝔼​hK​(g)=𝔼​‖g‖​w​(K)/2\mathbb{E}h_{K}(g)=\mathbb{E}\|g\|\,w(K)/2. Thus G=GΔG=G_{\Delta}. Gram rigidity as in Section VI-C(a) identifies K=U​ΔnK=U\Delta_{n}. Orthogonal images conversely attain equality. ■\blacksquare

VII Conclusion

The equal-energy problem for n+1n+1 signals is now closed in a strong sense. To the optimality proved in [12], this paper adds the equality cases. Away from the regular simplex no equality occurs at any finite threshold, at any positive moment-generating parameter, or under any positive energy budget. Steiner’s counterexample [5] delimits the scope, showing that under an average-energy constraint the regular simplex is not optimal and no such rigidity can hold.

Boundary conditions are sharp and cannot be dropped. The threshold must be finite, the moment-generating parameter strictly positive, the energy strictly positive, since each formal endpoint produces a trivial equality. All arguments admit singular correlation matrices. The case |Ri​j|=1|R_{ij}|=1 is handled inside the strict rectangle lemma.

Two directions remain. The pair-tail structure of the strict rectangle inequality is explicit and suggests a quantitative stability estimate, a deficit bound in terms of the distance from GG to GΔG_{\Delta}. For m≠n+1m\neq n+1 signals the optimal configuration is unknown in general, the rank-constrained problem posed in [12] included. The biorthogonal conjecture for m=2​nm=2n remains open.

the likelihood ratio of message ii against message 11. a function of TT alone. For every cylinder event BB the L1L^{1} convergence gives Pi​(B)=𝔼1​[𝟏B​Li]P_{i}(B)=\mathbb{E}_{1}[\mathbf{1}_{B}L_{i}].
